Why Investigate Surgical Patients Preoperatively?

Preoperative investigations identify conditions that may significantly affect surgical outcomes and recovery.

They provide crucial information that helps anesthetists and surgeons develop appropriate perioperative management plans.

However, 60–70% of routine laboratory tests ordered before surgery are unnecessary, resulting in:

  • Increased healthcare costs
  • Potential surgical delays
  • Resource inefficiency
Notes

1 · Why We Investigate Before Surgery

Preoperative investigation is not a ritual box-ticking exercise. Every test exists to answer a question about whether this patient can safely tolerate this operation — and what must be fixed first.

Identify risk factors
Uncover comorbidities and patient-specific hazards before they become intraoperative surprises.
→
Assess overall health
Establish baseline function and detect active medical problems, including undiagnosed disease.
Purpose of Preoperative Investigation
Optimize before operating
Control what is controllable — glycaemia, blood pressure, anaemia, electrolytes — while there is still time.
→
Improve outcome
Lower complication rates and reduce overall perioperative risk.
CORE CONCEPT
Investigation is the bridge between knowing the patient and operating safely. Its output is not a stack of results but a modified perioperative plan.

Guiding Principles for Preoperative Testing

Tests should be selective and purposeful, not routine.

Clinical History-Based

Tests should address specific concerns raised during comprehensive patient interviews about previous medical conditions, medications, and surgical history.

Physical Examination Findings

Abnormalities detected during physical assessment should guide targeted investigation rather than ordering a standard battery of tests.

Co-morbidity Assessment

Tests should be tailored to evaluate the impact of existing conditions on surgical risk and perioperative management.

Routine testing without clinical indication leads to inefficiency, unnecessary follow-up testing, and significantly higher healthcare costs with minimal benefit to patient outcomes.

Notes

2 · The General Approach

STEP 1 History·STEP 2 Physical Examination·STEP 3 Assess & Optimize Comorbidities·STEP 4 Selective Investigation

History

The same structured history used in any other specialty — surgery does not get a shortcut.

Chief complaint
History of presenting complaint

WORKED EXAMPLE
A patient with acute abdominal pain should be characterized systematically — site, onset, character, radiation, timing, associated features — then investigated. Ordering imaging first and thinking later produces random tests and missed risk factors.
Notes

Physical Examination

Focused and systematic, guided by the history.

RULE OF THUMB
History + physical examination are the two pillars that direct all further investigation. A good structured assessment produces purposeful tests; a poor one produces a scattergun of labs and imaging that still fails to identify the patient's real risk.

Common Preoperative Investigations

Complete Blood Count (CBC)

Renal Function Tests

Blood Glucose

Urea, Electrolytes, Creatinine assess kidney status and fluid/electrolyte balance critical for anesthesia safety.

Essential for diabetes screening/management as hyperglycemia increases infection risk and impairs wound healing.

Screens for anemia, infection risk, and platelet abnormalities that could affect surgical bleeding and healing.

Urinalysis

Chest X-ray & ECG

Particularly important before urologic procedures or any invasive surgeries to rule out urinary tract infections.

Indicated for patients with cardiopulmonary risk factors or those undergoing high-risk surgical procedures.

Notes

Assess & Optimize Comorbidities

Identifying a diagnosis is only half the task. The clinically decisive question is: is it currently controlled?

ComorbidityWhy it matters perioperativelyConsequence if left unoptimized
Diabetes mellitusPoor glycaemic control impairs wound healing and immune function.Worse procedural outcomes, ↑ complications, ↑ infection rates.
HypertensionUncontrolled BP destabilizes haemodynamics on induction and through the case.Anaesthesia may cancel or postpone the operation.
HIGH-YIELD TRAP
"The patient is diabetic" is not an assessment. "The patient is diabetic with an HbA1c of 11% and no recent review" is. A diagnosis alone is insufficient — always assess current severity and control.
Notes

3 · Preoperative Investigations

Investigations divide into two broad categories. Both must be organized and selective, never indiscriminate.

CategoryContents
1 · Laboratory testsCBC · coagulation profile · blood group, screen & crossmatch · renal function · liver function · glucose · chemistry/electrolytes · urinalysis
2 · Imaging & otherChest X-ray · ECG · targeted CT or MRI when indicated · PFTs · echocardiography
SELECTION IS DRIVEN BY
Patient factors — known disease, symptoms, age, comorbidities, functional status
Type and magnitude of the procedure — minor vs major, physiologic stress imposed
Organ system involved — and the expected effect of surgery upon it
Notes

Laboratory Tests in Detail

TestRationale / exam points
CBCPart of the general preoperative laboratory assessment — baseline haemoglobin, white cells, platelets.
Coagulation profileEspecially relevant in surgical patients because of perioperative bleeding risk, coagulation abnormalities such as DIC, and thrombotic risk.
Blood group, screen & crossmatchBlood group is determined; the number of units crossmatched is procedure-specific, driven by expected operative blood loss.
Renal functionBaseline for drug dosing, contrast exposure and fluid management.
Liver functionSynthetic function affects coagulation, drug handling and healing.
GlucoseCan detect previously undiagnosed diabetes — patients with no known comorbidity may still harbour active disease.
Chemistry / electrolytesCorrectable derangements that influence arrhythmia risk and anaesthetic safety.
UrinalysisScreens for occult infection and renal abnormality.

4 · Deciding Whether a Test Is Actually Needed

THE GOVERNING EQUATION
Patient Risk + Procedure Risk → Need for Further Testing
Neither axis decides alone. A high-risk patient having a trivial procedure and a healthy patient having a physiologically brutal one both need thought — but they need different tests.
Patient factorsProcedure factors
• Known disease
• Symptoms
• Age
• Comorbidities
• Functional / clinical status		• Minor vs major surgery
• Physiologic stress produced by the operation
• Expected effect on the relevant organ system
Governing equation: patient risk + procedure risk → need for further testing. Neither axis decides alone.
Notes

Applying It: Pulmonary Function Tests

AxisQuestions to ask
Patient riskKnown asthma, COPD or other pulmonary disease? Any pulmonary symptoms — particularly chronic cough? Symptoms may justify investigation even without a formal diagnosis.
Procedure riskMinor operation with minimal respiratory stress → PFTs usually not relevant. Major procedure such as open aortic surgery → significant cardiopulmonary stress → pulmonary assessment becomes important.
WHY POOR PULMONARY RESERVE MATTERS
Difficult or failed extubation
Unplanned ICU admission
Prolonged hospital stay
Pneumonia and other pulmonary complications
Notes

Applying It: Cardiac Testing

Whether to go beyond a baseline ECG — for example to echocardiography — is decided by exactly the same two axes: age, symptoms, comorbidities and overall patient risk on one side, major vs minor surgery on the other.

Notes

5 · VTE Prophylaxis

STUDENT-LEVEL RULE
Think about DVT/VTE prophylaxis in every single surgical patient. The form of prophylaxis then depends on individual risk — but the question is never skipped.
Patient-related riskProcedure-related risk
• Age
• Mobility
• Functional status
• Underlying thrombotic risk		• Type and magnitude of surgery
• Expected postoperative immobility
Clinical scenarioProphylaxis implication
Minor surgery, early discharge, mobile patientRelatively lower risk — early mobilization may suffice.
Major abdominal or colon surgery with postoperative immobilityIncreased DVT risk — requires pharmacologic prophylaxis.

WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: Enhancing Investigation and Safety

Pre-Anesthesia Check

Confirms patient identity, procedure, consent, site marking, and reviews critical investigations

Pre-Incision Timeout

Team introduces themselves, verifies patient/procedure again, reviews critical steps and anticipated issues

Post-Procedure Review

Confirms procedure performed, instrument counts, specimen labeling, and key recovery concerns

This 19-item checklist has been shown to improve teamwork, enhance communication, and significantly reduce surgical errors across diverse healthcare settings globally.

Investigating Surgical Site Infections (SSI)

Structured investigation tools help identify systematic lapses in infection prevention protocols when SSIs occur.

Key Data Points in SSI Investigation:

  • Detailed procedure information
  • Personnel involved in the surgery
  • Patient temperature maintenance
  • Appropriate bowel preparation
  • Timing and selection of prophylactic antibiotics
  • Skin preparation technique
  • Operating room traffic patterns

Systematic SSI investigation enables targeted quality improvement initiatives that can dramatically reduce infection rates and improve patient outcomes.

Preventing Wrong-Site and Wrong-Procedure Surgery

Site MarkingDocumentation
Surgeon marks operative site with indelible ink and patient verification when applicableConsistent labeling of all images, reports, and consent forms to prevent confusion
Timeout ProtocolCommunication
Final verification of patient, procedure, site, and implants immediately before incisionClear, standardized terminology and verbal confirmation between all team members

Root cause analysis reveals that communication failures are implicated in approximately 70% of wrong-site/wrong-procedure surgical errors.

Notes

6 · The Surgical Safety Checklist

PURPOSE
Prevent errors · confirm essential perioperative information · identify and address critical issues · improve outcomes. It is a whole-team responsibility — surgical, anaesthesia and nursing teams together, not the surgeon alone.
PHASE 1 Pre-Anaesthesia / Preoperative Check·PHASE 2 Intraoperative Time-Out·PHASE 3 Post-Procedure Review
PhaseWhat is confirmed
1 · Pre-anaesthesia checkPatient identity · correct procedure · consent completed · correct site marking (critical for paired structures — arms, legs) · review of important clinical issues.
2 · Time-outPerformed collectively by surgeon, anaesthesia and nursing. Reconfirms patient, procedure, consent, operative site, relevant prophylaxis including antibiotics, and critical patient/procedural issues. Team members actively verify — they do not simply listen.
3 · Post-procedure reviewProcedure actually performed · important operative details · whether it went as planned · complications · any additional interventions · extubation/intubation status · postoperative destination (ward vs ICU).
NON-NEGOTIABLE
Site marking and consent must be completed before proceeding in the OR — not retrofitted afterwards. Likewise, complications and important operative events must be clearly communicated and documented at the end of the case.
Notes

Critical Issues Raised During Time-Out

Severe COPD
Severe coronary artery disease
Expected procedure duration
Estimated blood loss
Blood availability / crossmatch
Planned anaesthetic technique
Expected difficulty with extubation
Expected postoperative disposition (e.g. ICU)

Raising these allows anaesthesia and the surgical team to modify the perioperative plan before harm occurs.

7 · Communication & Documentation

★ PROFESSOR'S EMPHASIS
These are among the most commonly missed and poorly performed aspects of surgical care — and they are examined precisely because they are neglected.
DomainWhat is requiredCost of failure
CommunicationClear exchange between surgical, anaesthesia, nursing and all other involved teams.Compromised patient safety and worse outcomes.
DocumentationAdequate recording of patient assessment, important perioperative decisions, procedure details, and complications/outcomes.Clinical and medicolegal problems.
CAREER ADVICE WORTH MARKS
Build good communication and documentation habits early. Repeated poor practice becomes very difficult to correct later.

WHAT QI DEMONSTRATES ABOUT YOU

Conclusion: Optimizing Surgical Patient Investigations

Evidence-based selective testing significantly improves patient outcomes while reducing unnecessary healthcare costs and potential delays.

Implementation of standardized safety checklists and infection investigation tools is essential for systematic quality improvement.

Effective multidisciplinary teamwork and communication are the foundation of error prevention in surgical settings.

Institutional commitment to following established guidelines ensures both patient safety and satisfaction.

"The right test, for the right patient, at the right time."

The four goals of preoperative investigation: identify risk factors, assess overall health, optimize, and reduce perioperative complications — not simply "run the routine labs".

History and physical examination are the two pillars that direct every subsequent investigation. Random assessment produces random testing.

A diagnosis is not an assessment — always establish whether the comorbidity is controlled. Uncontrolled hypertension can get the case cancelled; poorly controlled diabetes raises infection and complication rates.

The decision rule for any extra test: patient risk + procedure risk. Both axes, every time.

Coagulation studies matter in surgical patients for three distinct reasons: bleeding risk, DIC, and thrombotic risk.

Crossmatch is procedure-specific: minor surgery may need none; major open aortic surgery ≈ 4 units.

A preoperative glucose may reveal previously undiagnosed diabetes — absence of a known comorbidity does not mean absence of disease.

PFTs are justified by pulmonary disease or symptoms (especially chronic cough) plus a physiologically stressful operation; the feared consequences are failed extubation, ICU admission, prolonged stay and pneumonia.

Consider VTE prophylaxis in every surgical patient: early mobilization may be enough for low-risk minor surgery, while major abdominal/colon surgery with immobility requires pharmacologic prophylaxis.

The checklist has three phases: pre-anaesthesia check (identity, procedure, consent, site marking), intraoperative time-out (collective reconfirmation + antibiotic prophylaxis + critical issues), and post-procedure review (what was done, complications, disposition).

Consent and site marking must precede the operation, and site marking is especially critical for paired structures (arms, legs).

Communication and documentation are the most commonly neglected elements of surgical care, with both clinical and medicolegal consequences.
